Stage 3 · Language

What to say when you have not understood

Four moves. All of them buy you time, and none of them sounds weak.

Read these four lines from real job interviews.
  • I’m not sure I understand. Could you explain what you mean?
  • I’m sorry. Could you repeat that, please?
  • Do you mean what job will I have?
  • Oh, that’s a difficult question! Let me think…
Which one does something the other three do not?
Saying ‘I don’t understand’ stops the conversation. Naming the problem keeps it moving.

When you do not follow something in English, you have a choice between two very different moves. I don’t understand reports a general failure and leaves the other person guessing what to fix. Sorry, could you explain what you mean by ‘flexible’? isolates one word, keeps the exchange going, and makes you look attentive rather than lost. In an interview or a meeting, that difference is decisive.

There are three distinct requests hiding inside the vague phrase ‘I don’t understand’, and English keeps them separate. Repeat is what you ask for when you did not hear (Sorry, could you repeat that?). Explain is what you ask for when you heard but did not understand (Could you explain what you mean?). Example is what you ask for when you understand the words but cannot see how they apply (Could you give me an example?). Choosing the right one saves an entire round of misunderstanding.

There is also a move in the opposite direction: checking that you have understood correctly, by paraphrasing what the other person said and asking them to confirm. So, if I understand you correctly, the role involves travel? This is standard professional behaviour in English and is expected in interviews, meetings and phone calls.

The second half of the lesson, the application letter, rests on one principle worth stating before you see any phrases: replace adjectives with evidence. I am hardworking and motivated proves nothing, because anybody can write it. In my current role I manage a branch of twelve staff proves something, because it can be checked. Every claim you make about yourself should be followed by a fact in the next clause.

Before you look at the table: the tables below separate the clarification moves by what they actually ask for, then set out the letter skeleton. Note the word order in the clarification phrases — it is statement order, not question order.
The four moves
The moveWhat you sayWhat it does
Ask againCould you repeat that, please? · Sorry, could you explain what you mean by…?Puts the work back on the interviewer, politely.
Offer your versionDo you mean…? · So, if I understand you correctly,… · In other words,…Shows you were listening, and gets you a yes or a correction.
Buy timeLet me think… · Let me see… · That’s a difficult question.Two seconds of silence sound worse than four words.
Ask for an exampleCould you give me an example of that?Turns an abstract question into a concrete one.
Give one backTo give you a good example,… · What I mean is,…The same tools work when you are the one being unclear.

Do not just say “What?” or “Repeat, please.” Both are grammatically fine and both sound abrupt in English. The politeness lives in Could you…? and I’m sorry, not in the word please.

The strongest move is offering your own version. Do you mean what job will I have? tells the interviewer you are thinking, not lost. Notice the word order inside it: what job will I have — the reported question keeps statement order recycled from Lesson 12.

The mistake to avoid. Not What means “redundant”? but What does “redundant” mean? or What do you mean by “redundant”?

Written clarification exists too. In an email: Just to confirm my understanding,… or Could you clarify whether…? The same move, in a colder register.

Full grammar reference — asking for clarification, and the application letter

What it is

Two pieces of professional functional language. The first is the clarification set: how to say you have not understood, how to ask for an example, and how to check that you have understood correctly by paraphrasing. The second is the fixed structure and register of an application letter or email.

What it means, and what it does

Saying I don’t understand puts the problem on you and stops the conversation. Sorry, could you explain what you mean by ‘flexible’? puts the problem on one word, keeps the exchange moving and makes you look attentive rather than lost. In an interview this difference is decisive, which is why the phrases are worth learning as fixed units.

When and why we use it

When you do not follow something in English, you have a choice between two very different moves. I don’t understand reports a general failure and leaves the other person guessing what to fix. Sorry, could you explain what you mean by ‘flexible’? isolates one word, keeps the exchange going, and makes you look attentive rather than lost. In an interview or a meeting, that difference is decisive.

There are three distinct requests hiding inside the vague phrase ‘I don’t understand’, and English keeps them separate. Repeat is what you ask for when you did not hear (Sorry, could you repeat that?). Explain is what you ask for when you heard but did not understand (Could you explain what you mean?). Example is what you ask for when you understand the words but cannot see how they apply (Could you give me an example?). Choosing the right one saves an entire round of misunderstanding.

There is also a move in the opposite direction: checking that you have understood correctly, by paraphrasing what the other person said and asking them to confirm. So, if I understand you correctly, the role involves travel? This is standard professional behaviour in English and is expected in interviews, meetings and phone calls.

The second half of the lesson, the application letter, rests on one principle worth stating before you see any phrases: replace adjectives with evidence. I am hardworking and motivated proves nothing, because anybody can write it. In my current role I manage a branch of twelve staff proves something, because it can be checked. Every claim you make about yourself should be followed by a fact in the next clause.

Typical situations

You need the clarification language for interviews, meetings, phone calls and any conversation with a speaker you find fast or unfamiliar. You need the letter structure for any job application in English.

  • Signalling you have not understood — softened, and specific where possible.I’m not sure I understand. Could you explain what you mean by ‘target-driven’?
  • Asking for a repeat — when you heard nothing, rather than understood nothing.Sorry, could you repeat that, please?
  • Asking for an example — the most useful clarification move of all.Could you give me an example of that?
  • Buying thinking time — fillers that are acceptable in an interview.Let me think … That’s a good question.
  • Checking your understanding — paraphrase and confirm.So, if I understand you correctly, the role involves travel.
  • Rephrasing your own words — when the other person has not understood you.What I mean is, I’d like more responsibility. In other words, I’m ready to manage.
  • Opening an application — the fixed formula.I am writing to apply for the position of team leader.
  • Selling yourself — evidence, not adjectives.I believe I would be well suited to this role, having managed a team of six.

How it differs from similar structures

Could you repeat that? = I did not hear · Could you explain that? = I heard but did not understand · Could you give an example? = I understand the words but not how it applies.
Yours sincerely (you know the name) · Yours faithfully (Dear Sir or Madam) · Best regards (email, neutral–professional, not a formal letter).

How to build it

Not understanding: I’m not sure I understand. / Sorry, could you explain what you mean by + word?
Checking: So, if I understand you correctly, + clause
Rephrasing: What I mean is, / In other words, + clause
Application skeleton: greeting → the post and where you saw it → why you are suitable, with evidence → what you would bring → availability → close + sign-off
Clarifying a wordCould you explain what you mean by ‘X’? — note the statement order after what.
Clarifying a questionDo you mean what job I’ll have, or what I want to achieve?
Asking for a repeatSorry, could you repeat that? · Sorry, I didn’t catch that.
Asking for an exampleCould you give some examples of that?
ConfirmingSo you’re saying that…? · If I’ve understood correctly,…
Application — openingI am writing to apply for the position of…, advertised on…
Application — evidenceIn my current role I am responsible for… · I have three years’ experience of…
Application — closePlease find attached my CV. I would be happy to attend an interview.
Sign-offYours sincerely, (you named them) · Yours faithfully, (Dear Sir or Madam)

Usage notes and exceptions

  • After what you mean by, keep statement word order: what you mean, never what do you mean. This is the embedded-question rule from Lesson 12.
  • Repeat and explain are not the same request. Repeat = say it again (you did not hear). Explain = say it differently (you did not understand). Choosing the right one saves a whole exchange.
  • Explain does not take an indirect object without to: explain it to me, never explain me it. The same applies to describe and suggest.
  • In an application letter, replace adjectives with evidence. I am hardworking proves nothing; I increased sales by 15% in my first year does.
  • Do not use contractions in a formal application letter. Write I am, I would, I have.
  • Please find attached my CV is the standard formula. I attach my CV is also fine; I attached you my CV is not.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Could you explain what do you mean? → Could you explain what you mean?Statement word order after what.
  • Please explain me this word. → Please explain this word to me.Explain requires to before the person.
  • I write to apply the position of team leader. → I am writing to apply for the position of team leader.Apply takes for, and the continuous is standard here.
  • I have experience in manage teams. → I have experience in managing teams.After a preposition, the -ing form.
  • I am interesting in this position. → I am interested in this position.-ing describes the thing; -ed describes the person.
  • Dear Sir or Madam, … Yours sincerely, → Dear Sir or Madam, … Yours faithfully,Sincerely needs a name in the greeting.

More examples in context

  • not understandingI’m not sure I understand. Could you explain what you mean?
  • clarifying a wordSorry, could you explain what you mean by ‘target-driven’?
  • asking for a repeatSorry, could you repeat that, please? The line isn’t very clear.
  • asking for an exampleCould you give me an example of a typical week?
  • thinking timeThat’s a difficult question. Let me think…
  • checkingSo, if I understand you correctly, the role involves supervising four people?
  • rephrasingWhat I mean is, I work best when the goals are clear.
  • application openingI am writing to apply for the position of team leader, advertised on your website.
  • evidenceIn my current role I am responsible for a branch of twelve staff.
  • closingPlease find attached my CV. I would be happy to attend an interview at your convenience.

A tip for remembering it

For clarification, name the exact problem: a word (what you mean by…), the whole point (could you explain that again?) or the application (could you give an example?). For the letter, follow one rule throughout: every claim about yourself must be followed by evidence in the next clause.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Ask about a specific word: Could you explain what you mean by…? — statement word order after what.
  2. Repeat = I did not hear; explain = I did not understand; example = I cannot apply it.
  3. Check understanding by paraphrasing: So, if I understand you correctly,…
  4. Explain / describe / suggest + something + to + somebody.
  5. Open an application with I am writing to apply for the position of… and use no contractions.
  6. Back every claim with evidence; end with Yours sincerely (named) or Yours faithfully (Dear Sir or Madam).

Stage 5 · Main input

The letter that gets the interview

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what gets somebody an interview?

Choose one. The model does two of these and deliberately avoids two.

Subject: Application for the position of Assistant Manager (ref. HR-114)

Dear Ms Whelan,

I am writing to apply for the position of Assistant Manager advertised on your website on 2 March.

I have worked in customer service for four years, the last two as a team leader at Kensington Retail, where I supervise a team of six and am responsible for the weekly schedule. In that time our branch has moved from fifth to first in the regional satisfaction ratings, which I am told is the fastest improvement the company has recorded.

I believe I would be well suited to this position for two reasons. First, I already have the management experience the advertisement asks for. Second, I have been looking for a role in an expanding company where I can continue to make progress, rather than do the same job in a larger building.

Please find attached an up to date copy of my CV. I would be glad to discuss my application at any time that suits you.

Yours sincerely,
Amina Serikova

What the model does, in five moves
  • Names the position and where she saw it, in the first line. No warm-up sentence.
  • Gives one number — fifth to first. A claim you could check beats three adjectives.
  • Gives exactly two reasons. One looks thin; five look desperate.
  • Says what she wants next, not only what she has done.
  • Never says how much she wants the job. The letter shows it instead.
